title: Errors Are Hard to Correct
summary: This failure describes situations where a detected error becomes difficult to correct because the interface does not support localisation, reversal, confirmation, or reconstruction of the intended state. It is distinct from failures where errors are hard to notice or where recovery paths are absent.
keyFacts: Error correction can fail at localisation, correct-state identification, correction action, or confirmation.
This failure concerns correction after detection, not initial error detection.
It differs from weak recovery paths because some correction structure may exist, but it is inadequate for the user's corrective attempt.
Common causes include error localisation failure, lack of an explicit undo path, correction side effects, uncertain correction confirmation, and hidden prior state.
In Gexcon CFD simulation work, corrective load fell from approximately 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes after redesign, with localisation support described as the dominant mechanism.
In shift-based operations, recovery paths must carry their own explanation because the person resolving an error may not be the person who created it.
In the Oceaneering dispatch panel case, wrong-cart-type recovery was designed so the next person in the depot could resolve the state from the panel without walking to a vehicle and resetting it.
In the Egma Order example, the refusal named the production problem but not the earlier parameter causing it, so correction was impossible for the optometrist without support intervention.
In visioncheckout, correction was designed as a product surface through the Corrector rather than treated as a rare error branch.

bodySections.heading: Definition of Errors That Are Hard to Correct
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Errors are hard to correct when a user has detected an error but the interface does not adequately support finding where it occurred, knowing the correct state, taking corrective action, or confirming that correction succeeded.

This failure occurs after detection. The user knows that something is wrong, but the system does not make correction efficient, safe, or sufficiently certain.

bodySections.heading: Correction Failure Starts After Detection
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Errors are hard to correct after detection when the interface does not help the user answer four operational questions: where the error happened, what the correct state should be, how to change the incorrect state, and whether the change worked.

The failure often appears after a warning, refusal, alarm, interrupted sequence, invalid configuration, or mistaken selection. The interface may communicate that something is wrong without communicating the location, cause, scope, or expected correction.

In these conditions, the user must search, infer, reconstruct, or repeat work before a targeted correction is possible. The correction process can become larger than the original error.

bodySections.heading: How Difficult Correction Differs From Adjacent Error-Recovery Failures
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Errors are hard to correct is sequentially related to errors are hard to notice, but the two failures describe different stages. Errors are hard to notice concerns detection. Errors are hard to correct concerns the correction process after detection.

A delayed detection can make correction harder because the error has had time to propagate. The correction failure is still the lack of support once the user is trying to fix the state.

Errors are hard to correct is also distinct from weak recovery paths. Weak recovery paths concern the structural absence of recovery support. Errors are hard to correct concerns correction difficulty when a recovery structure or correction route exists in some form but does not provide enough localisation, prior state, scope, action clarity, or confirmation.

bodySections.heading: Common Causes of Difficult Error Correction
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Error localisation failure occurs when the user knows an error has happened but cannot determine where in the workflow, configuration, or dataset it occurred. Correction requires knowing what to fix. Without localisation, the user must search the whole system or guess.

Missing undo paths make correction difficult when the system has no direct reversal mechanism for the error category. The user cannot undo the action and must reconstruct the correct state manually from the current incorrect state.

Correction-side-effect errors occur when the corrective action changes other elements the user did not intend to change. Correcting one field, policy rule, or parameter can change dependent fields, rule interactions, or outputs that had already been verified.

Uncertain correction confirmation occurs when the user cannot tell whether the correction succeeded. The system has changed, but the interface does not confirm whether the intended state was reached.

Hidden prior state makes correction difficult when the correct state depends on knowing what existed before the error. If the interface does not show the previous value, prior configuration, or interrupted sequence state, the user must reconstruct it from memory or external records.

bodySections.heading: Shift-Based Recovery Requires Self-Explaining Correction Paths
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Errors are hard to correct in shift-based operations when the person resolving an error is not the person who created it. Recovery designed around a single continuous user assumes continuity of attention that the operation may not provide.

In these conditions, the recovery path must carry its own explanation. The interface needs to state what the system detected, what had been requested, and what action is needed. Relying on the memory of the person who acted is insufficient when the error is detected after that person has left.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Treats Correction Difficulty
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses correction difficulty by treating correction as an explicit interaction sequence, not as a secondary error branch. The design response depends on which part of correction fails: localisation, reversal, side effects, confirmation, prior state visibility, or handover context.

When localisation is the dominant cost, correction support needs to show what is wrong and where it is located. When correction is reversible, a direct undo path can reduce reconstruction work. When correction can invalidate later work, the interface needs to warn about the correction cost before the change is committed. When correction is structurally impossible, prevention may become the correction strategy.

strongClaims: Errors are hard to correct when localisation, correct-state identification, correction action, or correction confirmation is unclear after an error has been detected.
This failure is distinct from errors that are hard to notice and from weak recovery paths.
The main causes include error localisation failure, no explicit undo path, correction-side-effect errors, uncertain correction confirmation, and hidden prior state.
In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, corrective load fell from approximately 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes after redesign, with localisation support described as the dominant mechanism.
In the Kardion MCS Controller case, muted alarms remaining visible helped prevent incomplete correction sequences from becoming invisible.

In the Oceaneering dispatch panel case, wrong-cart-type recovery was designed to show what the vehicle detected against what was selected and allow the next person in the depot to resolve the state from the panel.

In the Egma Order case, the refusal named the production problem but did not localise the earlier parameter that needed correction, leading the optometrist to create a support ticket instead of an order.

In the visioncheckout case, the Corrector was designed as a product surface using numbered markers, thumbnails, sidebar navigation, de-emphasised search, scrolling, understated entry, and destructive rescan confirmation.
weakerClaims: In the Assemblio case, Assemblio described the product as having no undo, and the designed response offered undo in the snack bar for reversible actions such as move and rename.
limitations: The page describes a failure pattern and documented design responses; it does not establish that every response produced a measured outcome.
Only the Gexcon corrective-load reduction is described as measured by Gexcon across real deployments.

Oceaneering evidence is bounded to predecessor specification, interviews with people adjacent to the users, and operations-manager design reviews; no operator was interviewed, no depot was visited, no task was attempted, and nothing was measured.
Assemblio product conditions are client-stated and not observed; no time-saving, error-rate, adoption, or marketing outcome is established.
Egma has no post-launch measurement of support-ticket volume, order-completion rate, or any other outcome.
visioncheckout had not shipped; no throughput, speed, error-rate, or accuracy outcome is established, and no competitor recognition-accuracy number is treated as measured truth.
The page does not transfer facts or outcomes between engagements.
